assessment_summary: The statement claims that every triangle-free graph is 4-colourable. This is false; it is a well-known result in graph theory that there exist triangle-free graphs with arbitrarily high chromatic numbers. Since the statement is false, any attempt to prove it must fail. I have provided the shift graph on 17 elements as an explicit counterexample.
counterexample:
Consider the shift graph G = (V, E) defined as follows:
Vertices V = { (i, j) | 1 <= i < j <= 17 }. (There are 136 vertices).
Edges E = { {(i, j), (j, k)} | 1 <= i < j < k <= 17 }.

1) G is triangle-free: an edge connects a pair ending in j to a pair starting with j. To form a triangle, we would need 3 mutually adjacent vertices. If we start with v1=(a,b) and v2=(b,c) with a<b<c, the third vertex v3 must be adjacent to (b,c), meaning it is either of the form (c,d) with c<d, or (y,b) with y<b. If v3=(c,d), it cannot be adjacent to (a,b) since b!=c and a!=d. If v3=(y,b), it cannot be adjacent to (a,b) since b!=y and b!=a. Thus, no triangle can exist.

2) G is not 4-colourable: Suppose for contradiction there is a proper colouring c: V -> {1, 2, 3, 4}. For each element m in {1, ..., 17}, define the set of colours A_m = { c(m, x) | m < x <= 17 }. Since A_m is a subset of {1, 2, 3, 4}, there are 2^4 = 16 possible subsets. By the Pigeonhole Principle, among the 17 elements, there exist u < v such that A_u = A_v. 
Consider the vertex (u, v) and its colour C = c(u, v). By definition, C is in A_u. Since A_u = A_v, C is also in A_v. This implies there exists some w > v such that c(v, w) = C. But (u, v) and (v, w) are connected by an edge, so they must have different colours, which contradicts c(u, v) = c(v, w) = C.

Thus, G is a concrete triangle-free graph that requires at least 5 colours, falsifying the statement.
